EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  
“Immigration, Skills, and the Labor-Market Outcomes of U.S. Natives, 1960-2000”

-------------------------------------------------
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
Chosen method: Shift–share Instrumental Variables (IV) estimator implemented in a two-way-fixed-effects panel of (education × experience) skill cells observed in five cross-sections (1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000).

Why IV?  
• Simple DiD that regresses native wages on the contemporaneous immigrant share is likely biased because immigrants self-select into skill cells where labor-market conditions are favorable.  
• A Bartik/shift–share IV exploits (i) exogenous year-to-year variation in total U.S. inflows from each origin country and (ii) the 1980 (or 1970) distribution of immigrants across skill cells, both predetermined with respect to 1990-2000 outcomes.  This generates quasi-random supply shocks that are plausibly unrelated to cell-specific demand shocks.  
• The panel dimension lets us difference out time-invariant skill-cell heterogeneity (cell FE) and economy-wide shocks (year FE).

Model  
First stage:  Mst  = π Predicted_Mst  + λs + λt + εst  
Second stage:  yst  = β Ṁst  + λs + λt + Xst γ + νst  
where yst is an outcome for native workers in skill cell s at time t, Ṁst is the 2SLS-fitted immigrant share, λs are skill-cell fixed effects, and λt are year fixed effects.

-------------------------------------------------
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  

Treatment variable (continuous):  
Immigrant Sharest  = (# foreign-born men in cell s at time t) / (total men in cell s at time t).

Treated units: Skill cells that experience larger positive shocks to Immigrant Share.  
Control units: Skill cells whose immigrant share changes little or falls.

Instrument (“shift–share”):  
Predicted_Mst = Σc ( Immigrantsc,s,1980 / Total_Immigrantsc,1980 ) × Total_Inflowsc,t  
where c indexes origin countries. The 1980 country-by-skill distribution is held fixed; only national inflows vary over time, providing the “shift.”

Timing: Five census/CPS cross-sections; no single “event date.” Identification relies on inter-period changes 1960→70→80→90→2000.

-------------------------------------------------
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  

A1. Relevance: Historical country-of-origin settlement patterns strongly predict actual cell-level inflows (first-stage F-stat ≫ 10).  
Plausibility: Documented in previous literature; can be tested.

A2. Exclusion Restriction: Conditional on year FE, cell FE, and controls, Predicted_Mst affects native outcomes only through actual immigrant inflows, not through other channels (e.g., trade shocks).  
Plausibility: Reasonable but not guaranteed. We will (i) re-estimate with alternative base years, (ii) drop the largest origin countries one-by-one (“leave-one-out”), and (iii) control for cell-specific industry composition to bolster credibility.

A3. No Differential Trends within Cells (after FE): Absent immigrant inflows, wages of different skill cells would follow parallel trends.  
Plausibility: Decent; supported by pre-1960 evidence. We can test using event-study leads.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-cell spillovers): An immigrant shock to, say, dropouts with 6–10 years of experience does not directly alter wages of college graduates with 1–5 years of experience except through general-equilibrium wage adjustments that are captured by year FE.  
Plausibility: Possibly violated; we will probe cross-elasticities and present aggregate-labor-supply decompositions.

-------------------------------------------------
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION  

T1. Endogenous reclassification of natives (native skill upgrading or migration across experience groups).  
Fix: Use birth-year cohorts to define experience so that a given native remains in the same cohort over time; check whether immigrant shocks predict changes in cohort size.

T2. Instrument contamination by demand shocks correlated with origin-country inflows (e.g., Mexican inflow driven by construction boom that also raises low-skill wages).  
Fix:  
• Include region-specific industry trends.  
• “Leave-one-out” instruments excluding the five largest origin countries.  
• Instrument with refugee inflows (exogenous to U.S. labor demand) in a robustness exercise.

T3. Heterogeneous treatment effects biasing 2SLS (late-never-taker issue).  
Fix: Present reduced-form and first-stage coefficients; complement IV with quantile regressions and an event-study that interacts shocks with decade dummies.

-------------------------------------------------
5. R CODE OUTLINE  

```r
# --- 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast FE + IV
library(ivreg)       # alternative 2SLS
library(sandwich)    # robust vcov
library(lmtest)

# --- 1. Data Loading ---------------------------------------------------------
# Assume a single stacked file: census_cps_1960_2000.csv
df_raw <- read_csv("census_cps_1960_2000.csv")

# --- 2. Variable Construction -----------------------------------------------
df <- df_raw %>% 
  mutate(
    # skill cell identifiers
    educ_cat = factor(educ_cat, 
                      levels = c("dropout","hsgrad","somecol","colgrad")),
    exp_cat  = cut(experience, breaks = seq(0,40,5), right = TRUE, include.lowest = TRUE),
    skillcell = interaction(educ_cat, exp_cat, drop = TRUE),
    
    # immigrant dummy
    immigrant = if_else(birthplace == "US", 0, 1),
    
    # annualized real earnings
    lny = log(real_annual_earnings),
    
    year = as.integer(year)
  )

# Aggregate to cell-year level
cellyr <- df %>% 
  group_by(skillcell, year) %>% 
  summarise(
    n_total   = n(),
    n_imm     = sum(immigrant),
    n_native  = n_total - n_imm,
    lny_native= mean(lny[immigrant==0], na.rm = TRUE),
    lnw_native= mean(log(real_weekly_earnings[immigrant==0]), na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_work = mean(frac_weeks_worked[immigrant==0], na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(
    mshare = n_imm / n_total
  )

# --- 3. Build the Shift–Share Instrument ------------------------------------
# Load national inflows by origin × year
nat_inflow <- read_csv("national_inflows_country_year.csv")  # variables: country, year, inflow

# 1980 immigrant distribution by country × skillcell
base_year <- 1980
base_dist <- df %>% 
  filter(year == base_year, immigrant == 1) %>% 
  group_by(country, skillcell) %>% 
  summarise(n_base = n()) %>% 
  group_by(country) %>% 
  mutate(share = n_base / sum(n_base)) %>% 
  ungroup()

# Create predicted inflow for each cell-year
predicted <- expand_grid(skillcell = unique(base_dist$skillcell),
                         year = unique(nat_inflow$year)) %>% 
  left_join(base_dist, by = "skillcell") %>% 
  left_join(nat_inflow, by = c("country","year")) %>% 
  mutate(flow = share * inflow) %>% 
  group_by(skillcell, year) %>% 
  summarise(pred_M = sum(flow, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% 
  ungroup()

cellyr <- cellyr %>% 
  left_join(predicted, by = c("skillcell","year")) %>% 
  mutate(pred_mshare = pred_M / n_total)      # scale

# --- 4. Main 2SLS Regression -------------------------------------------------
est <- feols(lnw_native ~ mshare | skillcell + year ~ pred_mshare, 
             data = cellyr, weights = ~n_native, vcov = "hetero")
summary(est)

# First stage F-stat
summary(est)$iv_first_stage_F

# --- 5. Robustness: Leave-one-out Instrument --------------------------------
# Example: drop Mexico
predicted_LOO <- base_dist %>% 
  filter(country != "Mexico") %>% 
  # proceed as above ...
  group_by(skillcell, year) %>% 
  summarise(pred_M = sum(flow, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% 
  ungroup()

cellyr <- cellyr %>% 
  select(-pred_mshare) %>% 
  left_join(predicted_LOO, by = c("skillcell","year")) %>% 
  mutate(pred_mshare_LOO = pred_M / n_total)

est_LOO <- feols(lnw_native ~ mshare | skillcell + year ~ pred_mshare_LOO,
                 data = cellyr, weights = ~n_native, vcov = "hetero")
summary(est_LOO)
```

-------------------------------------------------
6. EXPECTED RESULTS (PRIOR)  

Theory (simple CES two-skill model) implies that an exogenous increase in the supply of a given skill lowers its relative wage. Empirically, I expect:  
β ≈ –0.3 to –0.6  (elasticity form).  Concretely, a 10 pp rise in a cell’s immigrant share should reduce native weekly wages by roughly 1–3 percent.  Employment (fraction of weeks worked) likely falls modestly (β ≈ –0.05 to –0.10).

-------------------------------------------------
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (IV)  

C1: Instrument relevance (first-stage F > 10) ………………… 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction plausible ………………………………… 0.5  
C3: No differential trends (parallel trends) ……………………… 0.8  
C4: No cross-cell spillovers (SUTVA) ……………………………… 0.5  
C5: Correct functional form / robust SEs ………………………… 1  

Total ≈ 3.8 / 5.  I judge the design credible but not bullet-proof; main weakness is the exclusion restriction and potential spillovers, which we partially mitigate with robustness checks and alternative instruments.
